newsitem.title: UK: Liver, not muscle, limits athletes, experts say.
newsitem.headline: Liver, not muscle, limits athletes, experts say.

text.p: Athletes are limited in how far and long they can run, cycle or swim not by the restrictions of bone or muscle but because major organs take up too much energy, American biologists suggested on Wednesday. Livers, kidneys and the stomach are the key to controlling metabolism, biologists Jared Diamond and Kimberly Hammond of the University of California wrote in the science journal Nature.
They said the most any person could increase metabolism was about five-fold and gave as an example cyclists competing in the Tour de France who burned 7,000 calories a day.
"The highest measured daily energy budgets maintained by any humans over long periods were achieved in the 1984 Tour de France race.
"For 22 days the world's best cyclists, in peak physical condition and fanatically motivated, pedalled up and down 34 mountains and over 3,826 km (2,377 miles)," they wrote.
The basal metabolic rate (BMR), or amount of calories burned just by existing, of a 70-kg (150-lb) man is 1,640 kcal a day. So a rate of 7,000 calories is about five times BMR.
The cyclists ate so much that none lost any fat, meaning they had an even intake and output of energy.

Diamond and Hammond said they wondered why the Tour de France cyclists were unable to train their bodies to do better. "If any of those athletes had been able to digest 17,000 kcal a day instead of 7,000, and convert it to muscular work, he would have left his competitors behind in the dust."
To see why this never happened, Hammond and Diamond checked the metabolic rates of 50 other animals. None could do much better than the cyclists.

Mice forced to run on a treadmill collapsed with exhaustion after six hours, no matter how much food was available and no matter how much they trained, which suggested there is a limit on how much fuel a living creature can convert to energy.
They noted that birds living in temperate zones, which have to deal with cold winters, had bigger hearts, kidneys, livers and intestines than tropical birds.

"These central energy-supplying organs, although their masses contribute only a modest fraction of an animal's total body mass, contribute a large fraction of an animal's resting metabolic rate," they added.
"For instance, in laboratory mice the kidneys have a mass-specific metabolic rate 51 percent higher than that of any other tissue."

They proposed looking at the organs of athletes to see if their kidneys and livers were proportionately bigger. Knowing the source of metabolic limits could help in sports medicine and in other types of medicine such as treating burns, which heal better when metabolic rate is increased.
